Fun fact: this book was first published in Iran, which then went on to ban the book shortly afterwards, presumably out of similar sentiments to those that made rivers of blood flow at the Charlie Hebdo offices. A Zahir according to Coelho is an all-consuming obsession. In Arabic it supposedly just means "the obvious" or "conspicuous". But for whatever reason Coelho seemed to avoid the issuance of religious kill orders like Salman Rushdie, so on with the show.

This is the second Coelho book I've read. The first, like most middle-class Westerners, was The Alchemist -- back when I was still a lot more amenable to magical thinking books like The Secret than I am now. I still have a soft spot for the book. It's basically as magical thinking should be put: a short fable that lets the reader draw from it what he may without getting humorously literal about itself. It has a certain magic to it, and a lot of beautiful heart.

The Zahir, by contrast, is basically four hundred pages of Coelho taking us on a voyage up his own anal tract. His protagonist is an author who is very, very much like himself, complete with several successful bestsellers that sound a lot like Coelho's previous novels. Then, one morning, poof, the author's wife disappears without a word. Coelho's protagonist then goes on a journey to rediscover himself on the way to dealing with his obsession with his absent wife and -- eventually -- to finding her again.

But the protagonist just comes across as plain old contemptuous to me. He says his wife was the love of his life but brushes off his own adultery (and hers) without so much as a word. I guess I could be all postmodernist and edgy and defend the book as saying "There are lots of people who fuck other people but still love their spouses" ... yeah, well, no. Coelho says all marriages are built on the two partners being "free" to "be themselves". I say all real marriages are built on trust and faith, and if you're willing to break both with your spouse, your marriage has either ended or you were never in one to begin with. If -- as it appears -- this is meant to be Coelho talking about himself I don't think he's the sort of man I'd like to know.

That, of course, is my politics and my personal makeup speaking. Can't do much about that. The real problem I think the book has is that Coelho chose the wrong literary device to tell it. He chose realism. This story would have been far better envisioned as an actual fable. Written as it is I find the protagonist neither sympathetic nor empathetic -- and it's the latter that counts far more. I simply cannot identify with a man who is self-obsessed like the protagonist is. Had Coelho's character been a knight in Game of Thrones I perhaps could have bought it. Not in a book that purports to capture the real world.

Snippets of the book are interesting, but those snippets did not deserve to go into a novel. They are far better suited to a copy of The Secret, or perhaps The Tenth Insight.

To be honest, the best part of the book is not written by Coelho. The story is prefaced with the poem Ithaca by C.P. Cavafy, which references, on its surface, the journey of Odysseus on the way home from Troy to return to his beloved, patient wife Penelope:

When you start on the way to Ithaca,

wish that the way be long,

full of adventure, full of knowledge.

The Laestrygones and the Cyclopes

and angry Poseidon, do not fear:

such, on your way, you shall never meet

if your thoughts are lofty, if a noble

emotion touch your mind, your body.

The Laestrygones and the Cyclopes

and angry Poseidon you shall not meet

if you carry them not in your soul,

if your soul sets them not up before you.

Wish that the way be long,

that on many summer mornings,

with great pleasure, great delight,

you enter harbours for the first time seen;

that you stop at Phoenician marts,

and procure the goodly merchandise,

mother-of-pearl and corals, amber and ebony,

and sensual perfumes of all kinds,

plenty of sensual perfumes especially;

to wend your way to many Egyptian cities,

to learn and yet to learn from the wise.

Ever keep Ithaca in your mind,

your return thither is your goal.

But do not hasten at all your voyage,

better that it last for many years;

And full of years at length you anchor at your isle

rich with all that you gained on the way;

do not expect Ithaca to give you riches.

Ithaca gave you your fair voyage.

Without her you would not have ventured on the way.

But she has no more to give you.

And if you find Ithaca a poor place,

she has not mocked you.

You have become so wise, so full of experience

that you should understand already what

these Ithacas mean.

(This is not the version that appears in the book. I prefer a different translation of the poem.) This poem states The Zahir's theme better, more concisely, and with more feeling than Coelho summons up in a few hundred pages. Stick to The Alchemist, it'll give you more than this one does.
